content: The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) has established specific recommendations for emergency egress from elevated workstations. Compliance with these standards is intended to prevent injuries or fatalities caused by insufficient egress facilities, lack of familiarity with emergency procedures, inadequate identification or illumination of escape routes, unawareness of imminent danger, or physical/medical conditions that impair a worker's ability to use egress systems effectively. The standard defines a unit of exit width as a 22-inch-wide segment of a standard means of exit. Fixed, portable, or job-made ladders that meet construction standards are considered one unit of exit width. The requirements for egress are determined based on the occupancy load of the workstation. For example, fixed ladders must comply with OSHA regulations (29 CFR 1910, 1926), and portable or job-made ladders must meet similar standards. Elevated workstations 15 feet or more above the ground or floor level, in low-hazard situations with an occupancy load of 10 or more employees, must have at least two means of egress. In high-hazard workplaces, where obstructions may impede escape, at least two means of egress are required regardless of the number of employees. Egress facilities must always be available and usable, even in buildings under construction. These facilities may include doorways, walkways, and other items specified in the standard. Emergency egress facilities must be positioned to minimize travel distances. Workers should not have to travel more than 100 feet to the nearest egress point, except in high-hazard situations where the maximum distance is reduced to 75 feet. Emergency alarm systems must be provided in workstations where fire or other emergencies may not provide adequate warning to workers. These alarms should alert workers to the emergency and facilitate orderly evacuation. These instructions must be printed in English and the predominant language of non-English-speaking workers, if applicable. Illiterate workers must also be informed of the procedures. Escape routes must be clearly marked or arranged to make the path unmistakable, with arrows or Exit signs as necessary. The minimum illumination level along the entire egress path must be at least 5 foot-candles, with provisions for maintaining this level during power failures. The psychological and physical effects of emergency egress situations have been studied. Stress during emergencies can significantly reduce operational efficiency, with some studies showing a loss of up to 90% in group performance. To mitigate this, egress systems should require minimal decision-making, be simple to use, and align closely with commonly practiced procedures. Research has shown that demonstrations and instructions alone are often insufficient for effective emergency response. Well-learned instructions are more likely to be retained over time, and proficiency during initial training is critical for long-term retention. In summary, the development of emergency egress systems must consider human behavior patterns, psychological stress, and physical limitations.
